paragraphs.text: The Great Tit (Parus major) is a widespread and common species of bird found in all types of woodland throughout Europe, the Middle East, Central and Northern Asia, and part of North Africa. It is generally resident in one place: most Great Tits do not migrate except in extremely harsh winters. Until recently this species was grouped with numerous other subspecies. However, DNA studies have now shown these other subspecies to be distinct from the Great Tit, and they have been classified as two separate species: the Cinereous Tit of Southern Asia, and the Japanese Tit of East Asia. The Great Tit remains the most widespread species in the genus Parus.

One of the first things to notice about the Great Tit is its size: it is larger than other tits. This fact may be related to its foraging behaviour. The Great Tit is less agile than the other tits, and spends more time feeding from the ground, a behaviour often seen in the autumn when there are plenty of fallen seeds. Its larger size also means that the Great Tit tends to be dominant over the other species, often evicting them from the tree holes and spaces which it then uses as nesting cavities.

Although male and female Great Tits appear superficially similar, a difference can be observed in the black stripe that extends down the chest and belly. In male birds this passes between the base of the legs. In females the stripe is reduced in width and does not reach the base of the legs. In addition it often contains some pale feathering, giving it a more washed-out appearance. In males the main plumage colours tend to be brighter and glossier than they are in females. As is the case in many other species, the plumage colours tend to get stronger with age. Prior to their autumn moult, young birds can be recognised by their pale yellow, rather than white, cheeks and by the different colour of some of their wing feathers.

Great Tits usually nest in tree cavities, and the female constructs the nest alone. She begins by building a substantial base of moss, with the addition of some grass and other plant fibre. Regardless of the floor space available within the cavity, she will cover the entire area with the same depth of material, so if the cavity is large the task is considerable. A nest cup is then added, lined with fur, wool, hair and other soft materials (though rarely feathers), into which the eggs will be deposited.

Once egg-laying begins, the female will usually lay one egg on a daily basis, though she may occasionally miss a day, something which is more common in early nesting attempts than in later ones. Egg-laying takes place early in the morning, after which the female covers the eggs with nesting material and spends time with her mate, before returning to the nest in the evening to roost.

There is a close association during this period between male and female. The male is busy protecting his mate from other male birds, and will often feed the female, contributing roughly a third of her daily intake. Given the amount that the female has to invest in each egg, this additional food may be particularly important. Each egg is between 1.3 and 2.3 grams, and represents roughly 10% of the female’s body weight, so a complete set of eggs is normally heavier than she is.

Incubation does not begin properly until all the eggs have been laid, so the presence of the female roosting overnight on the eggs does not necessarily mean that it has started. There is insufficient warmth for the incubation to begin unless the eggs are brought into contact with the female's brood patch, a small section of skin well-supplied with blood vessels that develops on her belly for that purpose.

Each Great Tit chick weighs roughly 1.5 grams at hatching, but by the time that the chick is able to fly away it is between 16 and 26 grams. This is a staggering increase, given that it takes place over a period of just three weeks. The amount of food needed to fuel this growth is equally staggering: for example, thousands of caterpillars are delivered to a typical brood of chicks raised in mature oak woodland. These dominate the Great Tit chicks’ diet, contributing some 60 to 95%, depending on the habitat, but their numbers fluctuate throughout the year.

Great Tits do better if they can match the period of peak demand from their chicks with periods of caterpillar abundance. However, research shows that climate change is affecting the Great Tits’ egg-laying pattern. In Britain, for example, they are laying their eggs an average of eight days earlier than they did in the 1960s, in response to warmer springs. Caterpillars are also emerging earlier, but the date on which they do so is influenced by temperatures experienced after the birds have already produced their eggs. By then there is little that the birds can do to advance hatching, so chicks may be produced too late, resulting in their reduced growth rates and even starvation. If this imbalance continues, it may have long-term implications for the Great Tit.

Great Tits are less at risk from predators than most other tits.
Other species of tit generally give way to the Great Tit.
The central black stripe on a Great Tit’s body is wider in the female than in the male.
The Great Tit’s colouring normally fades as it gets older.
The average number of eggs produced annually by the Great Tit is higher than it was in the past.
